expectedText:
CROWN ACT: RACE-BASED HAIRSTYLE DISCRIMINATION IN HIRING — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · Acme Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes how California's Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) defines "race" for purposes of its hiring-discrimination prohibition, and how that definition -- commonly associated with the CROWN Act amendments to Government Code section 12926 -- applies to Acme Inc.'s consideration of Jane Doe as an applicant for Marketing Coordinator. Government Code section 12926 states that "race" is inclusive of traits associated with race, including hair texture and protective hairstyles such as braids, locs, and twists, and Government Code section 12940(a) makes it an unlawful employment practice, subject to stated exceptions, for a covered employer to refuse to hire a person because of race. This document states facts about what those two statutory provisions say and whom they cover; it does not evaluate any particular grooming policy, application, or hiring decision. This corpus separately includes a document addressing FEHA's religious dress and grooming accommodation requirement under a different part of the same definitions section, Government Code section 12926(q), which covers hair, clothing, and other practices connected to an individual's observance of a religious creed and the accommodation duty that observance can trigger. That document addresses a religious-accommodation obligation; this document addresses a definition of "race" that does not depend on, and is not limited to, religious observance. This document is not itself a job application, a job posting, a grooming or dress-code policy, an offer of employment, or a determination of whether any specific policy or decision complies with the statutes described, and it does not tell Acme Inc. or Jane Doe what to do about any particular hiring decision, application, or workplace policy.

"RACE" IS DEFINED TO INCLUDE HAIR TEXTURE AND PROTECTIVE HAIRSTYLES
FEHA's definitions section, Government Code section 12926, states that as used in the part of the Government Code containing FEHA's unlawful-practices provisions, "race" is inclusive of traits associated with race, including, but not limited to, hair texture and protective hairstyles. This definition supplies the meaning of "race" wherever that term is used in FEHA's unlawful-practices provisions, including the hiring-related prohibitions in Government Code section 12940.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Race” is inclusive of traits associated with race, including, but not limited to, hair texture and protective hairstyles."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(w) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12926(w) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12926.)
  Known gap: The statute states that race is "inclusive of traits associated with race" and names hair texture and protective hairstyles as examples, but its text does not itself list, or supply a general test for identifying, any other traits that might likewise be "associated with race" beyond the two it names.

"PROTECTIVE HAIRSTYLES" INCLUDES BRAIDS, LOCS, AND TWISTS
The same definitions section separately defines the term "protective hairstyles" used in the race definition above. It states that protective hairstyles includes, but is not limited to, such hairstyles as braids, locs, and twists.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Protective hairstyles” includes, but is not limited to, such hairstyles as braids, locs, and twists."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(x) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12926(x) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12926.)
  Known gap: The list of example hairstyles in the statute -- braids, locs, and twists -- is expressly non-exhaustive ("includes, but is not limited to"), but the statute's text does not state a general definition of what makes a hairstyle "protective" beyond naming these three examples, so its text alone does not resolve whether a hairstyle not on this list falls within the term.

FEHA'S REFUSAL-TO-HIRE PROHIBITION APPLIES TO RACE AS SO DEFINED
FEHA's general unlawful-practices provision states that it is an unlawful employment practice, unless based upon a bona fide occupational qualification or an applicable security regulation established by the United States or California, for an employer, because of a person's race (among other listed characteristics), to refuse to hire or employ the person or to refuse to select the person for a training program leading to employment. Because Government Code section 12926 defines "race" to be inclusive of hair texture and protective hairstyles, this refusal-to-hire prohibition incorporates that definition wherever "race" is the basis asserted for the employer's action.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "It is an unlawful employment practice, unless based upon a bona fide occupational qualification, or, except where based upon applicable security regulations established by the United States or the State of California:"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12940(a), introductory clause (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  "For an employer, because of the race, religious creed, color, national origin, ancestry, physical disability, mental disability, reproductive health decisionmaking, medical condition, genetic information, marital status, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, age, sexual orientation, or veteran or military status of any person, to refuse to hire or employ the person or to refuse to select the person for a training program leading to employment, or to bar or to discharge the person from employment or from a training program leading to employment, or to discriminate against the person in compensation or in terms, conditions, or privileges of employment."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12940(a), refusal-to-hire clause (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  Known gap: Section 12940(a) states a "bona fide occupational qualification" exception and a security-regulation exception to the prohibition it states, but its own text does not define what qualifies as a bona fide occupational qualification or otherwise state how, if at all, either exception applies to a hairstyle-related job qualification; this document does not resolve that question, and the same section's text also does not itself define "refuse to hire."

WHICH EMPLOYERS THE FEHA DEFINITION OF "EMPLOYER" COVERS
The same definitions section that defines race states which entities are an "employer" for purposes of FEHA's unlawful-practices provisions, including the refusal-to-hire prohibition described above. It states that employer includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities, and it separately excludes a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit from that definition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Employer” includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12926(d), general employer definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12926.)
  "“Employer” does not include a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12926(d), religious-association exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12926.)
  Known gap: The statute's text does not itself state how the "five or more persons" threshold is counted -- for example, over what time period, in what location, or whether part-time or out-of-state personnel are included -- leaving that computation to sources outside this section's text.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to indicate receipt and review of this information sheet.

Applicant/Employee: Jane Doe
Position: Marketing Coordinator
Date: _______________

Acme Inc. certifies that this information sheet was provided to Jane Doe.

Company representative: _______________
Date: _______________
